math.prompt: An early skip is a skip within 30 seconds of starting a track. On autoplay, 180 of 900 starts with a fully observed window skipped early. In a manually opened mix, 30 of 300 mature starts did. Another 50 starts per surface are too recent to classify. If the target launch mix is 25% autoplay and 75% manually opened, estimate its early-skip percentage from the mature cohorts.
math.explanation: The mature rates are 180 / 900 = 20% for autoplay and 30 / 300 = 10% for the manually opened mix. Weight them by intended launch traffic: 0.25 × 20 + 0.75 × 10 = 12.5%.

walkthrough: Let each producer submit its best eligible titles. Build the screen by repeatedly selecting the row with the highest incremental value after removing already displayed titles, then recheck regional rights at delivery. Cache row candidates longer than the rights signal and backfill from the next eligible item on expiry. Greedy selection fits a tight deadline but can sacrifice a better combination of later rows.
title: Compose the first screen of a film festival app
brief: A streaming festival has a small catalog with staggered regional rights. The TV app displays labeled rows such as Recently Added and Documentary. Row producers supply scored, overlapping candidates. Design the page composer that chooses which rows to show and which films occupy the limited visible slots.
inputs: Each request has a region, row and slot limits, and eligible title proposals from row producers. A rights service independently declares which titles may be played in that region. A title can appear in multiple proposed rows.
outputs: Return ordered rows containing ordered title IDs. The first screen must contain no duplicate title, unavailable title or empty row. If fewer rows are feasible, send a shorter page. Row and title scores are model preferences, so multiple valid pages can exist.
why: T1 is unavailable in west and T3 can occupy only one slot. This example gives New first choice. Another valid composer could move T3 to Documentary if its page objective favors that placement.
constraints: Compose up to 6 rows of 8 titles from 25 proposed rows within 110 ms at p95.
Serve 900,000 profile opens/day in 12 regions. Rights changes must be enforced within 2 minutes.
One fifth of the catalog premieres every week. Evaluation must separately report titles with fewer than 100 historical impressions.

math.prompt: A streaming service can add B or C beside title A. In a cohort of 10,000 sessions, 380 users would consider watching A, 330 would consider B and 240 would consider C. Among them, 250 would consider both A and B, while 100 would consider both A and C. A session is covered if it contains at least one title the user would consider. By how many percentage points would C beat B as the second title?
math.explanation: A+B covers 380 + 330 − 250 = 460 sessions. A+C covers 380 + 240 − 100 = 520. The difference is 60 / 10,000 × 100 = 0.6 percentage points.

walkthrough: Filter the bounded pool using current club membership, mutes, visibility and event expiry before scoring. A light ranker combines estimated usefulness, freshness and impending deadlines. Freeze a ranked list of IDs for pagination, then recheck eligibility and remove shown IDs for each subsequent page. This keeps pagination predictable but can delay new notices until the next refresh.
title: Rank a campus clubs feed before events expire
brief: A campus app supplies recent posts from a student’s clubs. A popular debate can attract reactions for days while a useful room change matters for an hour. Design a ranker for the supplied pool that gets time-sensitive information to people while respecting explicit mutes.
inputs: The ranker accepts the viewer’s joined and muted clubs, request time, requested page size, and candidate posts with club ID, visibility, expiry, and optional engagement features. All times use UTC. Only active posts from joined, unmuted clubs are eligible.
outputs: Return an ordered list of eligible post IDs with no duplicates. Scores and ranking policy are design choices. Explain how cursors avoid repeated posts within a browsing session when new posts arrive.
why: All timestamps in the fixture are on the same day. The earlier chess notice has expired and drama is muted. Putting the room change ahead of the discussion is one feasible choice for the stated goal.
constraints: Rank at most 600 supplied candidates per request. Serve 4,000 peak requests/s at 80 ms p95.
Honor mutes and withdrawals within 15 seconds, including on paginated and cached feeds.
Only 3% of visible notices receive an explicit useful or unhelpful vote. Attendance confirmations arrive up to 48 hours later.

math.prompt: A feed ranker fans out to four scoring shards in parallel. Each independently responds before the deadline with probability 0.98. The usual ranking policy can serve if at least three shards respond on time. What percentage of requests can use that policy without a fallback? Round to two decimal places.
math.explanation: All four respond with probability 0.98⁴. Exactly three respond with probability 4 × 0.98³ × 0.02. Their sum is 0.99766352, or about 99.77%.

walkthrough: Apply cheap integrity checks and modality-specific classifiers first, then combine calibrated risks under the active policy. Auto-decide well-supported cases and route ambiguous cases to language-aware queues with an appeals reservation and backlog alarm. Log every disposition as an event linked to the evidence, and use an independent random audit to estimate misses among published clips. Stricter hold thresholds can reduce immediate exposure while increasing wait times, so test against actual reviewer capacity.
title: Triage multilingual clips with a finite review queue
brief: A community highlights app accepts short clips that combine images, speech and captions supplied by the creator. The policy team gives you labeled examples and a versioned rulebook. Design an upload decision service and human review queue for a launch in three languages. Editors can appeal a decision.
inputs: An upload has a clip ID, media references, optional transcript, detected language, arrival time and policy version. The example shows the calibrated component scores available after feature extraction. A routing decision may require missing evidence.
outputs: Return a disposition of publish, hold_for_review or remove with a policy version and internal reason code. A held clip stays unpublished until resolution. Explain how a later appeal updates the recorded decision without erasing the previous one.
why: One defensible policy sends conflicting evidence in an under-validated language to a specialist. The scores alone do not justify automatic removal. Other routing choices require explicit calibration and harm assumptions.
constraints: At peak, 80,000 clips arrive per hour. Six reviewers can each resolve 40 clips/hour, including appeals. Reserve at least 10% of capacity for appeals.
Issue an initial disposition within 8 seconds at p95. At least 95% of held clips should receive a decision within 2 hours during steady operation.
Audit a random sample of 1,000 published clips per week and report estimates separately for each launch language, including uncertainty.

tasks.title: Budget review decisions
tasks.prompt: Calculate the largest steady-state share of uploads eligible for review after the appeal reservation. Decide how to allocate that capacity by uncertainty, severity, language and age.
tasks.check: 216 new review slots/hour covers at most 0.27% of peak uploads before headroom. Address arrival bursts and specialist bottlenecks rather than treating the bound as a safe target.

tasks.title: Calibrate three actions
tasks.prompt: Specify which labels and policy versions train the baseline, how you combine conflicting modalities, and how you set class- or language-specific thresholds.
tasks.check: Define asymmetric error costs and report precision of automatic removal plus harmful prevalence among published clips. Include a missing-transcript path and threshold validation on held-out data.

tasks.title: Close the appeal loop
tasks.prompt: Diagram the immutable decision history from upload to appeal. Explain how overturned decisions and randomly audited published clips enter evaluation.
tasks.check: Record model, policy, timestamps and reviewer outcomes. Distinguish biased appealed examples from a random audit and prevent repeated uploads of the same clip crossing the test split.

tasks.title: Watch for harm during rollout
tasks.prompt: Choose a staged release plan and a rollback trigger. Estimate how many audit labels reach a low-volume language and explain what you can infer from zero observed misses.
tasks.check: Show why zero observed misses can leave substantial uncertainty, and specify how a targeted oversample would be reweighted or reported separately.

math.prompt: A moderation queue receives 30,000 uploads per hour. Twenty reviewers can each finish 12 cases per hour, and 25% of their capacity is reserved for appeals. A disjoint audit queue already consumes 30 of the remaining reviews per hour. What maximum percentage of all uploads may the model refer for new manual review while keeping mean demand at or below the remaining capacity?
math.explanation: The team can complete 240 cases per hour. After reserving 60 for appeals and 30 for audits, 150 slots remain. The mean-load ceiling is 150 / 30,000 × 100 = 0.5%. Running below it leaves room for arrival spikes.
